newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president clamps down on parliament, court.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president clamps down on parliament, court.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko on Thursday overturned decisions by parliament and the constitutional court which aimed to block his bid to tighten his grip on power through a controversial referendum this month.

But a leading parliamentarian, accusing Lukashenko of going "right over the top", said the deputies would not be intimidated by the increasingly authoritarian president's threat to dissolve the legislature and the court if they continue to oppose him.
Some analysts say they fear a showdown between president and parliament similar to that in Russia in 1993, when President Boris Yeltsin ended a legal stalemate with tanks.
The Belarus parliament -- backed by a court ruling -- voted on Tuesday that a referendum on increasing the president's powers, planned for November 24, would not be legally binding.
A senior presidential aide announced on television that Lukashenko signed a decree on Thursday saying he would dissolve parliament and the court if they failed to bow to his will.

"It (the decree) cancels, suspends the illegal decision of the Supreme Soviet (parliament) and the ruling of the constitutional court. From today they do not apply," Mikhail Sazonov, first deputy head of Lukashenko's administration, said.
The decree seemed bound to escalate a long battle between Lukashenko and the majority of deputies.
"He went right over the top. It's completely wild and will bring nothing good. It is a primitive decision," Vasily Novikov, parliament's first deputy speaker, told Reuters.
"We made no mistakes. But the president is very nervous. We are not afraid of dissolution, or finding a padlock on the doors to parliament," he added.
Sazonov made clear they would have to give in, or face dissolution.

"I am sure the parliament, deputies are intelligent enough not to block the referendum," he said. "If anyone, any state body, interferes with the referendum, the activity of that body will be suspended."
Belarussians, attracted to Lukashenko's anti-crime, pro-Russia policies, are expected to approve his constitutional draft. He keeps a tight grip on the media.

The draft would allow him to recommence his five-year term -- effectively extending it by two years -- create an upper chamber of parliament partly appointed by him and appoint half the constitutional court and half the commission which monitors and organises elections.

Deputies have proposed their own draft for a referendum, which suggests having local leaders elected rather than appointed by Lukashenko. Another proposal, seen as unlikely to succeed, would abolish the presidency altogether.

Lukashenko has provoked the wrath of nationalists and intellectuals in big cities with his populist approach and derisory comments on the Belarussian language, a Slavic tongue close to Russian. But he enjoys broad support in rural areas.

Generally scathing of Western interests in reforming his republic, sandwiched between Russia and Poland, he has described NATO as a terrible monster and opposed nationalists with such force that two of their leaders sought asylum in the United States.

The decree was one of the toughest moves he has taken against parliament since taking the helm of Belarus in July 1994, when he won a landslide victory on a platform of fighting corruption and rebuilding some kind of union with Russia.

Parliament, taking a long weekend break to mark the November 7 anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik revolution which is still an official holiday across the former Soviet Union, will not have a chance to react to the decree until Tuesday.
